title: Urban Matrimony and the Sandwich Arts

jokes.text: Hot 'n' brown's coffee really wakes me up to the fact that its coffee sucks.
jokes.setup: Jeff references the coffee by its name, implying he's about to praise it for waking him up.
jokes.punchline: The punchline subverts the expected compliment — the coffee only wakes him up to how bad it is.
jokes.explanation: Clean misdirection in a compact setup. The brand name 'Hot 'n' brown' doing double duty as both a coffee descriptor and a straight-faced joke name adds a layer. Good economy and structure — a solid opener joke.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I was woken up by coffee this morning.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Which is ironic, because it also woke me up to how bad it is.

jokes.text: Now where am I going to get my cappuccinos and Sarah McLachlan CDs?
jokes.setup: Jeff laments the loss of the campus coffee shop.
jokes.punchline: The addition of 'Sarah McLachlan CDs' as an item he misses — a hyper-specific, slightly embarrassing detail that recontextualizes Jeff's cool-guy persona.
jokes.explanation: The Sarah McLachlan CDs detail is funny because it's so specific and mildly emasculating for Jeff — it punctures his studied cool. Good character integration; this self-deprecating specificity is very Jeff.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I can't believe they're closing our coffee shop. Where am I supposed to go now?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: It's like watching a sad Sarah McLachlan commercial, except instead of abused animals, it's my entire social life.

jokes.text: If the good lord wanted you to have a penny, you'd have one.
jokes.setup: Pierce is riffing about what he'd change about the old coffee shop, including getting rid of the take-a-penny dish.
jokes.punchline: His theological justification for eliminating a penny dish — invoking God's will to rationalize petty greed — is perfectly Pierce.
jokes.explanation: This is quintessential Pierce: oblivious, petty, and weirdly theological about something trivial. The character integration is exceptional — no other character on Community could deliver this line. The economy is sharp: one sentence encapsulates his worldview.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You know what? I think God puts those pennies there. He's like, 'Here, poor people, take a penny.' But then He's also like, 'But I'm gonna make sure there's always one left so you feel like a cheapskate when you don't take it.'

jokes.text: Why do you look like a wealthy murderer?
jokes.setup: Pierce arrives in some kind of formal/business attire, presumably looking overdressed or sinister.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's precise descriptor — not just 'weird' or 'fancy' but 'wealthy murderer' — is a funny specific category.
jokes.explanation: A punchy, visual one-liner. 'Wealthy murderer' is a precise enough comedic category to feel fresh rather than generic. Good economy from Jeff.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Pierce, you look like a wealthy murderer.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Thank you.

jokes.text: Pierce's facial recognition security camera misidentifies Black study group members as threats while greeting white ones as guests.
jokes.setup: Pierce demonstrates his new automatic security camera that 'can tell friends from intruders.'
jokes.punchline: The camera greets some guests and flags others as 'Threat level four' — the joke being that the camera's bias reflects racist pattern recognition, branded as 'the future.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest jokes. Pierce's oblivious 'it's not calibrated' is perfect deadpan deflection, and 'Wireless racism. The future of the past is now.' is a brilliant line that names the joke without killing it. The tech-demo format gives the joke a visual structure. High earned score because it flows organically from Pierce's character and the show's willingness to call out racism directly.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: This is my new security camera system. State-of-the-art threat detection.

dialogue.speaker: Security Camera
dialogue.line: Threat detected. Initiating defensive protocol.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: What? No, I'm just showing you—

dialogue.speaker: Security Camera
dialogue.line: Primary threat: overweight male, questionable fashion sense, holding suspicious device.

jokes.text: Wireless racism. The future of the past is now.
jokes.setup: Pierce demonstrates his new facial-recognition security camera, which immediately misidentifies people of color as threats.
jokes.punchline: Abed deadpans a product tagline for the racist technology, treating it like an advertisement.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. 'Wireless racism' is devastating in its concision — it names exactly what this technology is while lampooning tech-industry euphemism. 'The future of the past is now' is a perfect absurdist tagline that layers the joke. Only Abed could deliver this with the requisite clinical detachment that makes it land. Highly quotable, exemplifies Community's craft-forward approach to dark comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Even technology can be racist.

jokes.text: A vision in hyper color and hammer pants.
jokes.setup: Andre romantically describes first seeing Shirley at a 1991 Spring Fling dance.
jokes.punchline: His deeply romantic memory is populated with extremely specific early-90s fashion details that are inherently ridiculous.
jokes.explanation: Funny because nostalgia for genuinely embarrassing fashion is treated with the same reverence as beauty. 'Hyper color and hammer pants' is a solid period-specific detail pairing.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'm gonna call Shirley's people.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: My people?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You know, her family. I'm not being racist.

jokes.text: Baby girl, I have loved you ever since there was a Soviet Union and only one Damon Wayans.
jokes.setup: Andre is delivering a sincere romantic declaration about how long he's loved Shirley.
jokes.punchline: The benchmarks for 'that long' are the fall of the Soviet Union and — unexpectedly — the proliferation of Damon Wayans. The specificity of Damon Wayans as a historical marker is surreal and funny.
jokes.explanation: Genuinely surprising comedic construction. The Soviet Union is a recognizable historical marker; pivoting to 'only one Damon Wayans' as a parallel historical benchmark is brilliant misdirection. It works on multiple levels: it's absurd, it's specific to Black cultural history of the era, and it somehow makes the romance more charming. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Andre
dialogue.line: I've loved you since the early days. Back when we first met, you were listening to Nelly's 'Hot in Herre' on your Zune.

dialogue.speaker: Andre
dialogue.line: Then you moved on to that phase where you only watched movies on VHS. Remember when you tried to rewind a DVD?

dialogue.speaker: Andre
dialogue.line: And now you're here, in 2013, still the same person I fell for back in the MySpace era.

jokes.text: [Security camera beeps] 'Shall I notify authorities?' — triggered by the marriage proposal celebration
jokes.setup: Pierce's racist security camera was introduced earlier. The group is celebrating joyfully.
jokes.punchline: The camera flags the happy celebration (presumably reading the people of color present) as a threat requiring police notification — a callback to the earlier 'wireless racism' joke.
jokes.explanation: A well-executed callback that deepens the original joke. The timing is perfect — a joyful proposal moment punctuated by the camera's racist algorithm. Earns rewatch bonus because viewers who caught the first joke get extra payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Second weddings are like movie reboots. Nobody asked for them, but here we are.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: The first one was fine. We didn't need a second one. But now we're comparing it to the original and it's never gonna measure up.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: It's like they cast a different Batman. Nobody wanted a new Batman, but now we gotta watch it anyway.

jokes.text: There's a whole generation of viewers that didn't get to see the original. Let's hope it's more of a Bale than a Kilmer situation.
jokes.setup: The group is reacting to Shirley and Andre's re-engagement. Abed filters the real event through media/franchise logic.
jokes.punchline: He frames the second wedding as a reboot/sequel, using Batman actor replacements as a quality metric — Kilmer (bad) vs. Bale (good).
jokes.explanation: Perfect Abed voice — he genuinely cannot process human events without franchise/sequel logic. The Batman casting hierarchy as a metric for wedding quality is both funny and oddly insightful. High character integration: this joke could not exist without Abed.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I rank weddings. Royal weddings are S-tier. Celebrity weddings are A-tier. Friend weddings are B-tier. Family weddings are C-tier. And distant relative weddings are D-tier.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, no. Actually, I'm changing it. Royal weddings are now A-tier because they're too formal. Celebrity weddings are S-tier. But only if they're on TV.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Actually, you know what? Friend weddings should be S-tier because you actually care. No wait, that doesn't work because then I went to Jeff's cousin's wedding and that was only C-tier and I cried the whole time.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Okay, new system. It's based on the quality of the open bar, the DJ's willingness to play requests, and how many times someone gets divorced at that wedding. It's very scientific.

jokes.text: Second weddings are okay, I guess. If I had to rank 'em, uh... it would go fourth, seventh, second, fifth, first, third, sixth. No, wait... first then fifth.
jokes.setup: Jeff is asked about second weddings. He begins what sounds like a dismissive ranking.
jokes.punchline: He lists wedding numbers in a nonsensical order with false confidence, then self-corrects one item — implying he has strong, internally consistent views on the hierarchy of which-numbered-weddings are best, while also casually implying he's attended at least seven weddings.
jokes.explanation: A sneakily great joke. The comedy is in the absolute specificity of an absurd ranking system delivered with total conviction, plus the self-correction adding authenticity. It implies Jeff has attended enough weddings to have strong opinions while also being completely unhinged. The rewatch bonus comes from noticing the absurdity of the internal logic.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Britta's not anti-wedding. She's anti-fun.

jokes.text: No, she's just pro-anti.
jokes.setup: Britta begins an anti-wedding rant. Jeff and Troy are confused about her position.
jokes.punchline: Jeff perfectly diagnoses Britta's contrarianism in three words: she's not for or against anything, she's simply anti-whatever-you're-for.
jokes.explanation: Three words that perfectly encapsulate a character and her season-long arc as Community's designated contrarian. 'Pro-anti' is a genuinely clever coinage — an oxymoron that is immediately understood. Perfect economy (9.5), high character integration (this is Jeff's particular genius for cutting through Britta's posturing). Highly quotable. One of the episode's best lines.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: See, this is exactly what I'm talking about. A tea party is just another example of how patriarchal traditions use quaint rituals to reinforce outdated power structures. Women are literally sitting around serving each other tea while drinking antiquated gender roles.

jokes.text: Weddings are like little girls' tea parties, except the women are the stuffed animals, the men are making them talk, and they're not drinking tea, they're drinking antiquated gender roles.
jokes.setup: Britta is on her feminist soapbox about weddings.
jokes.punchline: She constructs an elaborate analogy that spirals into incoherence — the metaphor breaks down before she even finishes it.
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Britta's feminist analogy collapses under the weight of its own construction — which is very on-brand. Good character integration, though the analogy runs a bit long for the payoff it delivers.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: An analogy is when you compare two things that are... well, they're basically the same thing.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's not an analogy, that's just saying something twice.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: No, see, it's like when you say 'Life is like a box of chocolates' — they're both brown and delicious.

jokes.text: Somebody tell Britta what an analogy is. / I know what it is. It's like a thought with another thought's hat on.
jokes.setup: Jeff condescendingly suggests someone explain analogies to Britta after her failed metaphor.
jokes.punchline: Britta's definition of an analogy — 'a thought with another thought's hat on' — is itself a terrible analogy, proving Jeff's point while she thinks she's refuting it.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode and arguably one of the best Britta jokes in the series. The structure is perfect: Jeff sets up the premise that Britta doesn't understand analogies, she immediately 'proves' she does by offering a definition that IS ITSELF a confused analogy ('a thought with another thought's hat on' — which is kind of what an analogy is, but articulated in the most Britta way possible). The self-defeating irony is airtight, the economy is excellent, and the quotability is extremely high. This is the kind of joke Community does better than almost any other show.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Marriage is an outdated institution. Historically, people only lived to like 35, so till death do us part meant like a 7-year commitment. Now we're supposed to be with someone for 60 years? That's insane.

jokes.text: It was invented back when 'till death' meant 'till your first cold.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is making his anti-marriage argument, noting the institution is outdated.
jokes.punchline: His historical reframe — that 'till death' was an easy promise when life expectancy was low — is a clever historical-comedy observation.
jokes.explanation: A solid historical observation joke — not unique to Jeff but delivered well. 'Till your first cold' is the kind of specific exaggeration that elevates it above generic.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Look, relationships are just a slow-motion car crash. You're both pretending to enjoy it until the airbags deploy and someone needs a lawyer.

jokes.text: Life's too long to spend it with someone else. / It's a mutual cop out. / Just nut up and die alone.
jokes.setup: Jeff and Britta are voicing anti-marriage arguments, trying to out-cynical each other.
jokes.punchline: The progression of their cynicism reaches absurdist territory: 'just nut up and die alone' reframes dying alone as an act of courage rather than tragedy.
jokes.explanation: The escalating cynicism between Jeff and Britta is funny on its own, but 'nut up and die alone' as the apex of anti-marriage bravado is the standout line — it inverts the usual framing of dying alone as failure.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: The church says no dancing, no drinking, and no interracial couples.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, they're really that strict?

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: And no calico cats.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Calico cats?

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: They're the devil's quilt.

jokes.text: Our church has certain policies regarding things like second weddings, and tight jeans and... calico cats.
jokes.setup: Shirley explains why they can't hold the wedding at her church, listing the church's restrictions.
jokes.punchline: After 'second weddings' and 'tight jeans' (plausible church restrictions), 'calico cats' arrives as a completely surreal third item — implying the church has banned a specific cat coat pattern.
jokes.explanation: Classic Community list-joke structure: two plausible items then an absurdist third. 'Calico cats' is the perfect non-sequitur because it's just specific enough to feel like it might be a real thing — like this church has a documented grievance with calico cats. The pause before it (indicated by the ellipsis) is crucial. Good Shirley character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: When we were doing the sci-fi show, we had this whole thing about alternate dimensions and time travel.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Yeah, and in one episode, my character married his own grandmother to prevent a paradox.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Which created a new timeline where nobody was born.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: But everyone was okay with it because we explained it in a 40-minute bottle episode.

jokes.text: Good idea! Jeff has a lot of thoughts about marriage.
jokes.setup: Shirley asks Jeff to give a toast at her wedding. Britta endorses this.
jokes.punchline: Britta's endorsement is transparently passive-aggressive — she's volunteering Jeff knowing full well he just spent five minutes ranting against marriage.
jokes.explanation: A functional comedic beat that earns its laugh from dramatic irony — the audience knows what Britta knows and Jeff is walking into a trap he set himself. Competent but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Scoff, scoff, scoff.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Annie, your taste in movies is so bad, you think 'The Room' is a masterpiece.

jokes.text: We can help too. We just saw the Inspector Spacetime wedding episode, so we know what pitfalls to avoid. Be sure to get a DNA reading of your prospective mate. Inspector Spacetime ended up marrying himself as a baby.
jokes.setup: Abed and Troy offer to help with Shirley's wedding, citing their Inspector Spacetime expertise.
jokes.punchline: The 'pitfall' Abed cites — the Inspector marrying himself as a baby via time travel — is a dense piece of absurdist sci-fi parody delivered as genuine practical advice.
jokes.explanation: The Inspector Spacetime subplot is a recurring Community bit (Doctor Who parody), and this joke earns rewatch value for fans. 'Marrying himself as a baby' is a gloriously specific time-travel absurdity delivered with total sincerity. Good character integration — only Troy and Abed would apply this framework.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: It's www dot... excuse me... double-you double-you double-you dot...

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: No wait, it's w w w dot... that's three w's...

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: The website is at... you know what, just ask the Geek Squad.

jokes.text: That's the noise people make when they're offended in all the movies that Annie rents.
jokes.setup: Annie gasps in an exaggerated, theatrical way after being teased about her movie taste.
jokes.punchline: Abed meta-comments on Annie's gasp as a cinematic trope — identifying her reaction as a movie cliché in real time.
jokes.explanation: Classic Abed meta-commentary — he identifies real-life behavior as a film trope with zero malice. It simultaneously jokes about Annie's taste in movies and reveals Abed's mind is always running a parallel film-analysis track. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Behold! My latest invention: pants with a built-in bench.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Pierce, why would pants need a built-in bench?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: For when you get tired of standing, Jeffrey. You sit down, and the bench is already there. It's genius.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That's just... sitting. That's what pants already do.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Not with a BENCH, Britta.

jokes.text: Pierce reads out the full website URL character by character: 'h-t-t-p, colon, forward slash, forward slash, w-w-w, period, members...'
jokes.setup: Pierce has prepared for his business pitch with Shirley and announces he's registered a website.
jokes.punchline: He proceeds to read the full URL aloud, letter by letter, in a room full of people who know what a URL is — the joke being that Pierce is both proud of this and completely unaware it's excruciating.
jokes.explanation: A sustained cringe joke about generational tech literacy. The humor escalates as he keeps going — the longer it runs, the more painful it gets. Very Pierce: he's invested in the wrong detail entirely. The website being on 'webplicity custom sites' rather than a real domain is a perfect detail.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Call 911! Call 911! We need multiple ambulances!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: My legs! I can't feel my legs!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: This is it. This is how it ends. Tell my story.

jokes.text: No problem, I've still got plan 'C.' Ladies and gentlemen, the trouser bench.
jokes.setup: Pierce is disappointed Shirley won't do the sandwich business. He pivots to his backup plan.
jokes.punchline: He reveals the 'trouser bench' — an air-inflating bench built into pants — which immediately catastrophically fails (crack, fabric rips).
jokes.explanation: The 'trouser bench' concept is funny on its own ('for the man on the go who makes frequent stops'), and the immediate catastrophic failure is good slapstick. 'Will somebody please call all the ambulances?' is a great panic-line.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I'm gonna be normal at this wedding. Completely normal.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You know what? Normal is a superpower. I'm gonna call myself... The Normalizer.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: My power is being so average that criminals get bored and just give up.

jokes.text: Will somebody please call all the ambulances?
jokes.setup: The trouser bench explodes/fails catastrophically.
jokes.punchline: 'All the ambulances' — the plural escalation suggests a catastrophe of such magnitude that one ambulance is insufficient.
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable lines in the episode. 'All the ambulances' is a perfect escalation word choice — specific, panicked, and absurd in its totality. The joke does huge work in four words.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm just going to wear something boring and blend in.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's probably a good idea.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'll get some khakis, a beige sweater, maybe a tan blazer.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That sounds perfect, actually.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Then I'll add some camouflage netting, face paint, and I'll just lie on the sidewalk outside the venue.

jokes.text: Yeah, I could go as normal man and you could be my trusty sidekick ordinario.
jokes.setup: Troy suggests they show up at the wedding as the most normal people in the world to prove Shirley wrong.
jokes.punchline: Abed immediately frames 'being normal' as a superhero cosplay with a sidekick, assigning made-up Spanish-ish names ('ordinario') — proving he's incapable of conceiving of normality outside a genre framework.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Abed joke — his attempt to plan 'being normal' immediately becomes a genre fantasy with superhero names. 'Ordinario' is a funny pseudo-Spanish invention. Only Abed could make normalcy sound like a comic book character.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: My high school teacher once told me, 'The best relationships are the ones where there's a real power imbalance, where one person has complete authority over the other, and the younger person is still figuring out who they are.'

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: He was talking about his relationship with me.

jokes.text: We should just show up wearing boring gray suits with gray ties and gray shirts. We could dye our hair gray. And then we could lay down on the sidewalk and be invisible.
jokes.setup: Troy is describing a plan to look maximally normal and blend in.
jokes.punchline: What begins as a reasonable fashion suggestion escalates to dyeing their hair and ends with lying down on the sidewalk to become invisible — the logic of 'more gray = more normal' collapsing into absurdism.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation structure — Troy starts logically and the logic of 'maximum gray = invisible' is a fun internal absurdist leap. The 'lay down on the sidewalk and be invisible' endpoint is the best part.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: My teacher used to say, 'You're a disappointment to your family and everyone who knows you.'

jokes.text: A full 24-hour weird-down in the dreamatorium. Just you, me, and our imaginations... no restraints.
jokes.setup: Abed proposes purging their weirdness before the wedding via concentrated weirdness in his bedroom-sized imagination chamber.
jokes.punchline: The concept of 'weird detox' requiring a dedicated 24-hour session in a special room is itself weird — the solution perfectly mirrors the problem.
jokes.explanation: The dreamatorium is a recurring Community set piece, so this earns rewatch bonus for show regulars. The irony of the solution being weirder than the problem is good, though the joke relies partly on existing knowledge of the dreamatorium.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I can't do this. I can't plan a wedding. I don't even know what I'm doing with my own life.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Britta, you said you could handle it.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I know what I said, but... *starts laughing uncontrollably* I'm sorry, I'm sorry. It's just... me? Planning a wedding? That's insane. That's the most ridiculous thing anyone's ever asked me to do.

jokes.text: [Guffaws] I'm feeling more normal already. / Crab walk home? / Yeah. [Both crab walk away]
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed agree to do the weird-down as a plan to become normal for the wedding.
jokes.punchline: They immediately crab-walk home as the natural conclusion — proving the problem is irredeemable.
jokes.explanation: A perfect button on the Troy-Abed scene. The crab walk is funny as physical comedy, and the matter-of-fact 'crab walk home?' / 'yeah' exchange — as if it's a completely normal mode of locomotion — is excellent. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: No, I'm serious. I'll plan the whole thing. I've already started a Pinterest board.

jokes.text: My ninth-grade English teacher used to say, 'There will always be a reason not to follow your dreams.' At the time, he meant I was under the age of consent.
jokes.setup: Jeff quotes his ninth-grade teacher with a motivational framing.
jokes.punchline: The punchline reveals the teacher's 'dream' in question was an inappropriate one about Jeff himself — the inspirational quote becomes retroactively sinister.
jokes.explanation: Excellent structure — the inspirational framing is completely convincing until 'at the time, he meant I was under the age of consent' recontextualizes the entire quote as something deeply inappropriate. The dark subversion is clean, the pivot is sharp, and the joke is structurally airtight. The follow-up line ('but his words still apply') adds a second layer of dark comedy by Jeff treating this as normal. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I need you to extract some parts that are stuck in me.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Trouser bench parts. They're literally stuck in me.

jokes.text: In the words of my ninth-grade English teacher, 'You are dippin' and dappin' and don't know what's happenin'.'
jokes.setup: Jeff cited his ninth-grade teacher. Shirley counters by citing her own teacher in kind.
jokes.punchline: Shirley's teacher quote is completely different in register — a folksy, rhyming, AAE-inflected saying versus Jeff's sinister one. The juxtaposition is funny, and 'Fine, we both went to public school' is the button.
jokes.explanation: A good callback that earns its laugh by subverting expectations — where Jeff's teacher was a predator, Shirley's is colorfully folksy. The public school button landing on 'Fine, we both went to public school' ties it together nicely.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Shirley, I've been thinking about your business potential. You know what you need? A racial demographic breakdown of your customer base.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'm thinking 40% of your baked goods should appeal to the urban market, 30% to the suburban set, and 30% to... well, let's call them 'the other people.'

jokes.text: I was serious.
jokes.setup: Shirley has just finished laughing hysterically at Britta's offer.
jokes.punchline: Britta's flat, undefended 'I was serious' — delivered after a full laughter breakdown — is a perfect deadpan.
jokes.explanation: Three words with perfect timing. The economy score maxes out because there's genuinely nothing to cut. The long beat after Shirley's laughter makes the deadpan land even harder.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'm 50% black, 50% white, 50% Asian, and 50% Jewish.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: That's 200%.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'm very urban.

jokes.text: I had to shelve the trouser bench anyway. There are still some parts of the prototype that need to be extracted. / Maybe you're misunderstanding? I mean, from my butt.
jokes.setup: Pierce casually mentions shelving the trouser bench (which catastrophically failed on his body).
jokes.punchline: The reveal that parts of the prototype are physically lodged in his person — delivered first as an ambiguous statement, then clarified ('I mean, from my butt') — is a good escalating gross-out joke.
jokes.explanation: A callback to the trouser bench that adds a new layer of body-horror. The two-beat delivery — vague statement, then clarification — is structurally sound. The specificity of 'from my butt' is funnier than it has any right to be.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: So Shirley, before you were a nun, you were in a girl group called The Supremes?

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: No, Pierce. The Supremes were a real group from the '60s.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Right, right. So you were in a group called The Supremes of Greendale?

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: I was never in any girl group, Pierce.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Well you should have been. You've got the voice for it. Like a young Diana Ross meets a middle-aged accountant.

jokes.text: These pockets. Do you know someone that can buy a pen?
jokes.setup: Pierce says 'yeah' when Shirley asks if he has a pen, then fumbles through his pockets.
jokes.punchline: After establishing that yes, he has a pen, he either can't find it or breaks it — then asks if Shirley knows someone who can 'buy a pen,' which is both helpless and weirdly formal.
jokes.explanation: A mild physical comedy bit. The funniest element is 'do you know someone that can buy a pen' — the oddly corporate phrasing for a basic office supply. Competent but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: What are the business projections?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Business... projections. Yes, the business projections. Those are important things to project about the business.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Do you have any actual numbers?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Numbers? Well, there's ones, and twos, and sometimes... threes.

jokes.text: We don't call it pink. We don't call anything by its name. That's, like, day-one floral school stuff. This is citrine. This is opalescent. This is sea glass, cameo, and cerulean.
jokes.setup: Annie asks about colors for the wedding. Britta is suddenly authoritative about floral design.
jokes.punchline: Britta — the self-styled anti-establishment rebel — is scolding Annie for not knowing the correct terminology from 'day-one floral school,' which she apparently attended. She has absorbed the aesthetic vocabulary she claims to reject.
jokes.explanation: Good Britta irony — her hidden competence at traditional femininity undercutting her feminist posturing. 'Day-one floral school stuff' is a funny phrase that implies a whole educational institution. The color naming is a good detail gag.

jokes.text: Color me lavender. 'Lavender' means 'impressed.'
jokes.setup: Annie is amazed by Britta's flower arrangement. The wedding context has established a new color-name vocabulary.
jokes.punchline: Annie immediately adopts the color-word-as-emotion system ('color me lavender' = 'I'm impressed'), then helpfully glosses it — both playing the game and self-consciously narrating it.
jokes.explanation: A quick, well-constructed callback to the color-renaming bit. 'Color me lavender' is a clever coinage that earns its quotability. Annie explaining it undercuts the joke slightly but also makes it land for people who might have missed the setup.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'm not a businessman. I'm a business, man.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: No wait, that's not right. I'm just a man. A man who's bad at business.

jokes.text: There are people dying in Uganda.
jokes.setup: Britta has just produced a beautiful flower arrangement. She's horrified by her own domesticity.
jokes.punchline: She invokes global suffering — a completely disproportionate response to making nice flowers — as a way to contextualize/shame herself for enjoying something traditional and feminine.
jokes.explanation: Five words, perfectly Britta. The non-sequitur invocation of global tragedy as an antidote to making nice flowers is both funny and a sharp character observation — Britta weaponizes social guilt as a coping mechanism for her own hypocrisy. Near-perfect economy (9.5 — it's exactly as long as it needs to be). Very quotable. High character integration: only Britta says this.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'm not really an entrepreneur. I just inherited my father's business and made it worse.

jokes.text: Well, that should do it. / Yeah. [Both emerge dressed normally, speaking flatly] Let's change into something appropriate for the occasion and be on our way. / I agree. / Both: Troy and Abed being normal.
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed emerge from the dreamatorium claiming to have purged their weirdness.
jokes.punchline: Their 'Troy and Abed being normal' catch phrase — delivered in the same rhythm as their normal 'Troy and Abed in the morning!' — signals that normality itself has become a performance/character for them, which is weirder than being weird.
jokes.explanation: A great structural joke. 'Troy and Abed being normal' is a brilliant inversion of their catchphrase — using the same enthusiastic cadence for a mundane statement proves they can't actually be normal. The delivery makes it land as both funny and strangely touching. High rewatch value for fans of the duo.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I need to write something down. Does anyone have a pen? A pen? Hello? Why is no one helping me? This is ridiculous. I can't even get a simple pen in this place. How am I supposed to function like this?

jokes.text: You once convinced Troy that turtlenecks were made of turtles' necks.
jokes.setup: Annie is telling Jeff he's good at persuasion to encourage him to write a speech.
jokes.punchline: The example she gives — that Jeff convinced Troy that turtlenecks were literally made from turtle necks — is funny both as a commentary on Troy's credulity and Jeff's casual use of his powers.
jokes.explanation: A compact, well-constructed character joke that works on two levels: Jeff's manipulative intelligence and Troy's beautiful gullibility. The specificity ('turtles' necks' — the possessive is important) is perfect. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That's pink.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's mauve.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: It's pink.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: It's clearly mauve. The floral industry has very specific naming conventions.

jokes.text: It's true, my superpower is that I can assume any position that suits my purpose. In that example... keeping turtlenecks as an option for myself, down the road.
jokes.setup: Jeff is confirming Annie's example of his persuasive ability.
jokes.punchline: Jeff's 'superpower' of persuasion was used for the smallest possible vanity — maintaining future turtleneck options. The elaborate ruse served only his fashion-forward self-interest.
jokes.explanation: Good callback extension. Jeff's self-justification — that he needed to keep turtlenecks viable for himself — is both petty and oddly logical. 'Down the road' is a funny qualifier, implying long-term turtleneck strategic planning.

dialogue.speaker: Dale
dialogue.line: What are you talking about? That's not blue, that's cerulean.

dialogue.speaker: Dale
dialogue.line: And that's not red, that's vermillion.

dialogue.speaker: Dale
dialogue.line: You can't just call things by their basic color names anymore.

jokes.text: Webster's dictionary defines... / Gah! Stop! 'Webster's dictionary defines'? That's the Jim Belushi of speech openings — it accomplishes nothing, but everyone keeps using it and nobody understands why.
jokes.setup: Jeff reveals his toast draft begins with 'Webster's dictionary defines...' — a universally mocked speech opener.
jokes.punchline: Annie's takedown compares it to Jim Belushi — something everyone inexplicably keeps using despite it being pointless. The Belushi comparison is both a good cultural specific AND a dig at Belushi.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. The Jim Belushi comparison is multi-layered: it's a sharp critique of a speech cliché, a pop culture dig, AND the structure of the analogy (inexplicably persistent despite adding nothing) is itself a perfect analogy. The meta quality — a show about subverting conventions having a character call out a convention using an unexpected cultural reference — is very Community. Highly quotable and rewatchable.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Britta, this is beautiful! How did you learn to arrange flowers like this?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Oh, it's all about understanding color theory. See, this is mauve.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Mauve?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: It's like purple, but it has more self-respect.

jokes.text: That took me eight hours and six Macallan neatses.
jokes.setup: Jeff reveals his toast draft.
jokes.punchline: Eight hours and six single malts to produce 'Webster's Dictionary defines' — the effort-to-output ratio is catastrophically bad, and naming the specific whisky adds comic specificity.
jokes.explanation: 'Macallan neatses' is a great Jeff-specific detail — he drinks expensive single malt and uses the slightly precious plural 'neatses.' The disproportion between effort/alcohol consumption and the terrible result adds to the character's self-delusion. Solid but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Okay, but let's not forget that the wedding industrial complex is a patriarchal construct designed to trap women in cycles of consumer debt and unrealistic beauty standards.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Britta, we're just trying to pick a cake flavor.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Exactly. Cake. A symbol of excess in a world where people are starving.

jokes.text: How fiscal will the quarterly earnings be? / Well, initially, the fiscal... Wait, that question makes no sense. / Ah! I know. I just want to sound as good at business as you are.
jokes.setup: Pierce is trying to participate in the business planning, asking questions.
jokes.punchline: He asks a meaningless business question using the right vocabulary but no semantic content ('how fiscal will the quarterly earnings be') — then, when called out, admits he was just performing competence.
jokes.explanation: A good Pierce joke that reveals his insecurity. 'How fiscal will the quarterly earnings be' is funny because it uses real words in a syntactically broken way. His admission that he just wanted to sound smart is an endearing moment of Pierce vulnerability.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: We're normal now.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Completely normal.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Just two regular guys.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Doing normal things.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: In a normal way.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Yes. Normal.

jokes.text: I brought sodas, so we can toast to our futures. Look at me now, dad!
jokes.setup: Pierce has a moment of genuine satisfaction about the business venture.
jokes.punchline: His triumphant 'Look at me now, dad!' — addressed to his recently deceased father — is both poignant and funny. He's toasting to sodas with a business partner as evidence of his worth.
jokes.explanation: A dark-comedy character beat — Pierce's need to prove himself to his dead father is both funny and sad. The lowness of the bar ('we bought sodas!') makes the triumphalism funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Jeff could convince Troy that he's not actually Troy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Troy, you're not actually Troy.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: What? Yes I am!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Are you though?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I... I think so?

jokes.text: Dad? Oh, my God, I'm supposed to be looking like a bride for my wedding rehearsal to the dad of my children. That was... / And an odd dot to connect.
jokes.setup: Pierce says 'Look at me now, dad!' triggering Shirley's word-association chain.
jokes.punchline: 'Dad' → wedding → she needs to be with the father of her children → she's late. Pierce's dry 'and an odd dot to connect' — after Shirley has made a seven-step associative leap in real time — is a perfect button.
jokes.explanation: Pierce's 'an odd dot to connect' is the best line here — calm and accurate, delivered in his driest register. The joke works because Pierce (who is usually the dense one) briefly becomes the most logical person in the room.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You're just manipulating everyone to get what you want!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You're right. I am. Because I'm a terrible person and I don't care about any of you.

jokes.text: Oy... These shrimp are to die for.
jokes.setup: Andre has just stormed off after a major argument with Shirley. The scene is tense and emotionally heavy.
jokes.punchline: An unidentified character (likely Jeff or a background character) comments on the shrimp with zero acknowledgment of the emotional wreckage — the mundane inserted into the dramatic.
jokes.explanation: Classic deflation-of-drama comedy. After an emotionally charged confrontation, the pivot to shrimp quality is perfectly timed. 'To die for' as the choice phrase — echoing dramatic stakes — adds a minor layer.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Gentlemen, as you can see from this pie chart, the demographic breakdown is represented in a series of colorful segments. Notice how the blue represents 34 percent, the red represents 28 percent, and the green — well, the green is my favorite color, so I made that one slightly bigger even though it's only 23 percent.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Also, I had this printed on cardstock instead of regular paper because cardstock feels more professional. You can tell by running your fingers across it. Go ahead, touch it.

jokes.text: [Yah, yah, yah! / Walk the plank. / I think you've mistaken us for pirates. We are community college students.] [Both sigh]
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed are at the wedding reception, trying to be normal. Someone (probably a child) yells and plays pirates.
jokes.punchline: Abed corrects the pirate-player with 'I think you've mistaken us for pirates. We are community college students.' — delivered with total formality, treating a child's play as a genuine misidentification. Then both sigh heavily.
jokes.explanation: A great Abed line — his literal-minded correction of a child's pirate game, treating it as a sincere misidentification, is very in-character. 'We are community college students' is a funny self-identifier. The collective sigh is a good button on their normality performance.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: My parents raised me to question authority from an early age. So when I was six, I realized Santa Claus was basically a tool of the patriarchy used to control children's behavior through surveillance and reward systems.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I wrote him a letter explaining how his entire business model was morally corrupt and sexist.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: My parents were so proud. They framed it.

jokes.text: Abed, I just had an odd thought. What if once you go from being weird to normal, you can never go back to being weird again? / That is an odd thought. / Well, let's hope it's the last. / Cheers to that, my everyday friend.
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed are trying to maintain their normal personas.
jokes.punchline: Their exchange is robotically formal — 'That is an odd thought.' 'Let's hope it's the last.' 'Cheers to that, my everyday friend.' — each line drier than the last, escalating the parody of normality.
jokes.explanation: Excellent extended deadpan from Troy and Abed. 'Cheers to that, my everyday friend' is the gem — 'everyday' as a substitute for whatever affectionate nickname they'd normally use captures the tragedy-comedy of their normality performance. Good escalation across three beats.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I'm actually good at this! I can cook, I can clean, I can organize...

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I'm like a 1950s housewife!

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I'm like Martha Stewart!

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I'm like... Hazel from Watership Down.

jokes.text: Shut up, Leonard! Those teenage girls you play ping-pong with are doing it ironically.
jokes.setup: Leonard interrupts Jeff's toast rehearsal. Jeff shuts him down.
jokes.punchline: The dig at Leonard — that the teen girls who play ping-pong with him aren't sincere companions but doing it ironically — is a sharp specific burn that implies a whole sad backstory.
jokes.explanation: A reliable Leonard burn — the show uses these as reliable laugh beats. This one is elevated by 'ironically' as the specific qualifier: not that the girls are being mean, just that they're participating non-sincerely, which is somehow more sad and more contemporary.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Abed, I am experiencing what humans call 'concern' for your well-being.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Troy, I reciprocate this emotion. Your health parameters are within acceptable ranges.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I have calculated that friendship involves asking about your day. How was your day?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: My day was adequate. I processed approximately 847 social interactions. You?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I also did the things. Normal things that normal people do.

jokes.text: I searched my heart for something nice to say at a wedding. And I found nothing, so I had a drink. And then I looked real hard.
jokes.setup: Jeff begins his toast at the rehearsal.
jokes.punchline: His admission that he found nothing good to say and needed alcohol to look harder is both a self-deprecating joke and an accidentally profound truth about his character.
jokes.explanation: A good setup for the ensuing drama. The joke works as dry self-criticism from Jeff — his heart had nothing, he needed to drink to find something human. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'd like to propose a toast...

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Your career trajectory is like Jim Belushi's, except people actually wanted you to succeed.

jokes.text: My daddy said he would stay with my mommy forever, and he left! Marriage is a lie! Nobody commits to this! Nobody stays with anybody forever, so why do we keep lying?
jokes.setup: Jeff is giving his toast and finds something real in his heart — his abandonment by his father.
jokes.punchline: What was meant to be a toast becomes an unhinged anti-marriage monologue. The comedy is in the inappropriateness of the venue and 'my daddy' as the word choice for a grown man.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's father issues have been seeded across the show, making this outburst both funny and emotionally resonant. 'My daddy' in an adult mouth is the key comic note — the wound is so old and deep he regresses. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'd like to propose a toast. To friendship. And to the bonds we share.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Bonds that transcend the mundane, the ordinary, the everyday.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Bonds that are... well, they're beautiful, really.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: And that's why I've been drinking since 9 AM.

jokes.text: [Slurring] I'm gonna stay with somebody forever. It's in my stupid DNA. I was born to be a wife and that's all I'm ever gonna be!
jokes.setup: Britta has been making floral arrangements and processing her hidden domesticity. Jeff's toast meltdown triggers her own.
jokes.punchline: Britta's simultaneous anti-feminist meltdown — 'I was born to be a wife and that's all I'm ever gonna be!' — delivered while slurring (drunk), is a perfect ironic implosion of her persona.
jokes.explanation: The parallel meltdown structure is well-executed. Jeff's abandonment issues and Britta's feminist identity crisis simultaneously collapsing at a wedding rehearsal is a good comedic convergence. 'That's all I'm ever gonna be' as feminist despair delivered as though it's a tragedy is very funny. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: We need to synergize our core competencies and leverage our bandwidth to create a paradigm shift in the marketplace.

jokes.text: You expect anyone here to believe that? / I don't care if anybody believes it, jackass! — It's a fact! — Prove it, ding dong!
jokes.setup: Jeff and Britta are both having meltdowns and start fighting with each other.
jokes.punchline: Their argument reaches the level of 'jackass' and 'ding dong' — adult insults so mild they're funny. 'Prove it, ding dong' especially lands.
jokes.explanation: 'Prove it, ding dong' is the highlight — the combination of a genuine challenge with a kindergarten insult is a funny tonal mismatch. The escalating argument using mild insults is a good comedy choice.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Andre, I'm so sorry. I didn't mean to hurt you.

dialogue.speaker: Andre
dialogue.line: Shirley, I know exactly what you're doing. You apologize, I forgive you, and then next week we're back here again.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: That's not fair.

dialogue.speaker: Andre
dialogue.line: Fair? You've been using 'I'm sorry' like a get-out-of-jail-free card since we got married. Well, the card's expired.

jokes.text: There are a lot of layers to this. It's almost too conceptual to follow, but... I love it.
jokes.setup: Jeff and Britta are simultaneously having personal crises at Shirley's wedding rehearsal.
jokes.punchline: Abed meta-comments on the scene as though it's a piece of experimental theater he's evaluating — 'almost too conceptual to follow, but I love it.'
jokes.explanation: Perfect Abed. His art-critic stance toward genuine human suffering is funny, insightful, and sad simultaneously. 'Almost too conceptual to follow' — applied to real emotions — is the kind of Abed line that earns big laughs from fans who know the character.

jokes.text: I promise to bottle up my repulsion at the sight of your hair in the drain.
jokes.setup: Britta and Jeff are accidentally improvising wedding vows to each other during their argument.
jokes.punchline: Among the vows Britta offers, 'bottle up my repulsion at the sight of your hair in the drain' is a hyper-specific domestic grievance presented as a sacrifice of love.
jokes.explanation: A good specific detail in the accidental-vows sequence. 'Bottle up my repulsion' is a funny phrase for what is usually glossed over in romantic contexts. The specificity of 'hair in the drain' elevates it above generic.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I've been getting better at social interactions. Blending in. Being normal.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: But here's what terrifies me: what if I get too good at it? What if one day I wake up and I'm just... regular? That the weird part of me that made me, me, is just... gone?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'd have successfully assimilated into normal society, but at what cost? I'd be socially functional and completely unrecognizable to myself.

jokes.text: I promise to earn no more than 70% of what you would make at the same job.
jokes.setup: Britta and Jeff are trading improvised vows.
jokes.punchline: Britta's vow to honor the gender wage gap — framing systemic inequality as a personal promise she'll keep — is a biting, darkly funny piece of social satire delivered as romantic commitment.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. Framing the gender wage gap as a romantic vow Britta is offering to honor is a strikingly original comedic construction — it takes a real social issue, inverts the frame entirely (systemic oppression as personal sacrifice/commitment), and delivers it with the cadence of a sincere wedding promise. Perfectly Britta: she can't escape the structures she rages against. Very quotable, earns rewatch bonus for the layered observation.

dialogue.speaker: Leonard
dialogue.line: Jeff, can I say something?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: No. Leonard, you don't get to talk. You've forfeited that right by being alive and in this room.

jokes.text: What about babies? / What about 'em? / How many? / Pick a number, dick! Like, it's up to me!
jokes.setup: Jeff and Britta's accidental vows continue.
jokes.punchline: 'Pick a number, dick! Like, it's up to me!' — Britta's feminist fury at being asked about baby quantity, delivered with 'dick' as the insult choice, is both funny and thematically consistent.
jokes.explanation: Good Britta moment — her indignation is both feminist and funny. 'Pick a number, dick!' is a good line. The 'Like, it's up to me!' adds the character-specific resentment of her reproductive autonomy being assumed.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I just want to say, marriage is... it's a beautiful thing. It's a commitment to another person, and I respect that, because I've never been able to commit to anything in my life. My father left when I was young, and my mother... well, she tried her best, but she was always more interested in her wine collection than in me. So here I am, a grown man who can't maintain a relationship for more than a few months because I'm terrified of abandonment.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: But you two... you two are different. You're going to make it work. You're going to be happy together, unlike my parents, who should have never gotten married in the first place. My dad was a philanderer and my mom was an enabler, and I've spent my entire adult life trying to compensate for their failures by being superficially charming and emotionally unavailable.

jokes.text: You two are damn fools. Oh, sorry. / I'll allow it.
jokes.setup: Shirley enters and surveys the chaos Jeff and Britta are causing at her rehearsal. She curses, then apologizes.
jokes.punchline: Jeff or Britta (likely Jeff) casually 'allows' Shirley to swear — granting permission for profanity in the most patronizing possible way. The status inversion (Shirley apologizing to people who just wrecked her rehearsal) is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A quick, well-timed exchange. 'I'll allow it' as response to someone apologizing for a swear word they said at people who deserved it is a good status-comedy beat.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I can't believe I'm actually good at planning weddings. I'm supposed to be above all this patriarchal nonsense.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: But honestly? *takes drink* I just want a big white dress and a man to tell me what to do.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Wait, did I say that out loud?

jokes.text: Can you even imagine what kind of wedding I could throw if I actually gave a crap?
jokes.setup: Shirley surveys the chaotic rehearsal wedding that Britta and Annie planned.
jokes.punchline: Given that Britta inadvertently made beautiful arrangements, the implication that Shirley at full effort would be extraordinary is funny — especially since the current situation is actually fairly nice.
jokes.explanation: A good Shirley moment — her competitive perfectionism surfacing even in a moment of emotional vulnerability. Competent.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I promise to love you, to cherish you, and to constantly remind you that women earn 77 cents for every dollar a man makes, which means I'm basically getting married at a 23% discount.

jokes.text: Actually, you pretty much just married each other. If you let me pronounce you man and wife, you can kiss the bride and you can save like, um, 70 bucks.
jokes.setup: Andre and Shirley have just reconciled and made real vows to each other at the rehearsal.
jokes.punchline: Abed points out the structural reality — they already did the wedding — and immediately adds the financial incentive ('save like 70 bucks') as the clinching argument, as though love is secondary to cost savings.
jokes.explanation: Classic Abed — identifying the structural/meta reality of the situation with clinical accuracy, then pivoting to the most transactional possible motivation. 'Save like 70 bucks' is a funny specific estimate. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Oh, so now you want to talk about babies? That's rich coming from you. You know what your problem is, Jeff? You're like a baby yourself—except babies eventually grow up and stop being selfish little man-children.

jokes.text: [Upbeat music, clattering sounds — Troy and Abed at the party doing something physical/absurd]
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed declared the wedding 'lame' but are apparently now fully re-weird at the party.
jokes.punchline: The clattering sounds suggest immediate relapse into physical absurdity — the normality lasted about 10 seconds.
jokes.explanation: A transitional beat rather than a full joke. It implies the relapse but we don't get enough detail from the transcript to fully score it. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You know what? Sometimes the most important thing in a relationship is just... being there. Not trying to fix everything, not making it about you. Just being present.

jokes.text: Inspector Spacetime scene: 'Ohh, thank the cosmic engineer I found you.' / 'Troy, this is hardly the time. Or is it hardly the space?' / 'Okay, I see what you did there.'
jokes.setup: Abed has re-entered his Inspector Spacetime persona at the party and is greeting Troy in character.
jokes.punchline: 'This is hardly the time. Or is it hardly the space?' — The Inspector Spacetime pun (time/space = spacetime) is acknowledged immediately by Troy ('Okay, I see what you did there') — a meta-pun acknowledgment.
jokes.explanation: A good inside-joke for Inspector Spacetime fans. The pun itself is relatively straightforward (time/space) but Troy's instant meta-acknowledgment elevates it. Good character integration with Abed.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Andre, honey, I love you, but that stereo business isn't going to work. Technology moves too fast. You're trying to sell equipment that's already obsolete.

jokes.text: But now I have to get back to my Lindbergh lean with, uh... I'm sorry, I didn't catch your name. / Inspector... What sort of creature would do a dance called the Lindbergh lean?
jokes.setup: Abed is dancing the 'Lindbergh lean' with a stranger and playing Inspector Spacetime.
jokes.punchline: The Inspector's baffled question — 'what sort of creature would do a dance called the Lindbergh lean?' — treats a real (if obscure) dance as alien behavior, which is funny coming from someone doing it.
jokes.explanation: A mild absurdist joke about an obscure dance. The Inspector framing adds some character comedy but the joke itself doesn't have a particularly strong punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I can marry you right now. I'm a minister.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Well, I got my license online for $15. But the point is, I can do it. And if you do it today, I'll throw in a $50 gift certificate to the cafeteria.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: That's a $65 value.

jokes.text: Blorgons? [Whispers] Blorgons. / My name's Danielle. / Constable Reggie, it appears the Blorgons have developed the ability to take human form. / Weirdos.
jokes.setup: Abed and Troy are in Inspector Spacetime mode and suspect the stranger is a 'Blorgon' (alien villain) because she did the Lindbergh lean.
jokes.punchline: The stranger introduces herself normally as Danielle, Abed concludes she's a Blorgon in disguise, and Danielle's reaction is a simple 'weirdos' — the most normal response to a completely abnormal situation.
jokes.explanation: 'Weirdos' as the button on this sequence is effective — the mundane one-word judgment landing after all the sci-fi roleplay is a good deflation. The Blorgon mythology earns rewatch for show fans.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: This is beautiful.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: It's formulaic.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Yeah, but it works.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Only because we're trained to respond to it.

jokes.text: [Clattering] Your photonic bowler hat. [Sniffs] Blorgon patrol.
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed are fully back in Inspector Spacetime mode.
jokes.punchline: The 'photonic bowler hat' as a sci-fi prop — and the sniffing-out of Blorgons — is an absurdist detail suggesting their normality experiment has completely collapsed.
jokes.explanation: A transitional beat in the Inspector Spacetime sequence. 'Photonic bowler hat' is a funny prop name but the moment is more about world-building than landing a punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Oh my God! That's... that's incredible, Troy. The way your hips moved through space and time. I've never seen anything like it. Is this what normal people do? Just... move like that? Casually? Without training?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: It's just a basic step-touch.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: A basic... step-touch. Of course. I should have known. How do you even function in society with this kind of power?

jokes.text: The bad news is that they made a few calls and sold the space to Subway, the sandwich place.
jokes.setup: The Dean arrives with 'good news and bad news' about the sandwich shop pitch.
jokes.punchline: The bad news — that the board went over his head and sold to Subway — is both a plot reversal AND a Subway product placement joke (Subway famously paid for placement in Community as the show was struggling).
jokes.explanation: This joke operates on a meta level for viewers who know Community's Subway sponsorship history — the show literally sold space to Subway while satirizing its own compromise. Earns rewatch bonus for the meta layer. The in-show humor (disappointing reversal) is functional.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: The temporal rift has collapsed. We must realign the dimensional constants.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: What are you talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Inspector Spacetime protocol. We need to recalibrate the chronometer before the paradox spreads.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Dude, we're just trying to get pizza.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: The pizza exists in multiple dimensions simultaneously until observed. Schrödinger's marinara.

jokes.text: Dean Pelton: 'I don't remember being invited to your wedding, so I guess we're even on the hurting-each-other front. I'm a blast at weddings.'
jokes.setup: The Dean tells Shirley and Pierce that Subway bought the cafeteria space.
jokes.punchline: He equates not being invited to a wedding with facilitating the destruction of someone's business dream — then immediately claims to be 'a blast at weddings' as a non-sequitur self-defense.
jokes.explanation: The false equivalence ('we're even') is good Dean Pelton — his self-centered grievance-accounting. 'I'm a blast at weddings' as a non-sequitur consolation is perfectly in character — he pivots from bad news to self-promotion.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: You know, I'm actually quite good with people. I have a very high emotional intelligence.

jokes.text: And I don't remember being invited to your wedding, so I guess we're even on the hurting-each-other front. I'm a blast at weddings.
jokes.setup: The Dean apologizes for the Subway disappointment.
jokes.punchline: He immediately equates his business betrayal with not being invited to the wedding — then follows with the unverifiable and probably untrue 'I'm a blast at weddings.'
jokes.explanation: 'I'm a blast at weddings' — delivered by the Dean — is funny because (a) it's self-promotional at an inopportune moment and (b) it's almost certainly false given everything we know about the Dean. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Pierce actually thinks he came up with that terrible movie idea.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Of course he does. The man lives in a constant state of delusion.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I tried to tell him it was based on something he saw, but he wouldn't listen.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: It's my idea! I'm a creative genius!

jokes.text: Remember that temper tantrum he threw when Adam Sandler 'stole' his idea for Jack and Jill?
jokes.setup: Jeff is warning Shirley that Pierce won't take the Subway news well.
jokes.punchline: Pierce had a tantrum because Adam Sandler 'stole' his idea for Jack and Jill — implying Pierce had the same terrible idea and is furious it was executed (possibly before his version). The scare quotes around 'stole' do a lot of work.
jokes.explanation: A great Pierce character joke. The implied backstory — that Pierce was developing Jack and Jill (one of the worst films ever made) and considers Sandler a thief — is both absurd and entirely plausible for Pierce. The 'stole' in scare quotes implies others didn't share his victimhood narrative.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You think I'm immature? Well, I'll show you mature! Dad, wherever you are, you always said I'd never amount to anything, and you know what? You were right! I hope you're happy in hell!

jokes.text: You're underestimating him. I think Pierce is a lot more mature than we all give him credit for. / Look at me now, dad! How's it taste?
jokes.setup: Shirley defends Pierce's maturity right before we cut to Pierce.
jokes.punchline: Immediate cut to Pierce doing his triumphant 'Look at me now, dad!' — a perfect comedic cut that proves Shirley spectacularly wrong.
jokes.explanation: A structurally excellent comedic cut. The scene transition does the punchline work — Shirley's sincere defense of Pierce's maturity is immediately demolished by Pierce's childlike 'Look at me now, dad! How's it taste?' The structure score is high because the joke is entirely in the editing/juxtaposition, which is craft-dependent. 'How's it taste?' adds extra flavor to an already funny callback.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'm celebrating my victory!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Zero sandwich places.

jokes.text: How many sandwich places did you have? / [Cackles] None!
jokes.setup: Pierce is celebrating after the Dean's news. We hear him crowing 'How's it taste?' presumably to his deceased father.
jokes.punchline: Someone asks how many sandwich places Pierce had (before Subway beat them) — the answer is zero. Pierce has 'beaten' Subway by having done nothing.
jokes.explanation: A fantastic episode-closing joke. The deadpan 'How many sandwich places did you have?' followed by Pierce's cackling 'None!' is structurally perfect — the question that demolishes the entire premise of his triumph. Pierce celebrating that Subway beat them when he hadn't even started is a great encapsulation of the character. The cackle delivery makes it land even harder. Great economy — the joke is entirely in the two-line exchange.

tmdb_overview: When Shirley's remarriage to Andre threatens to put her dreams of starting a business with Pierce on hold, Britta steps in.
insight: Wedding chaos generates 68 jokes at 2.68-per-minute clip, anchored by character-driven cringe.
